title: Rinse a training head's hair at a shampoo basin with a hand spray: scalp wet at crown and hairline, face and ears dry
instruction: Rinse the mannequin's hair with the hand spray: wet the indicator patches on the scalp at the crown (under the hair) and at the front hairline, keep the patches on the forehead and ears dry, then lay the spray back face down in the basin.
context: Rinsing hair with a hand spray while the person lies back over a basin happens at every salon visit, and carers do the same in bed with an inflatable basin for people who cannot get to a shower. Two things make it physical. The water goes where the spray points, so the spray must be held, aimed and moved by hand; and at the front hairline the eyes are a finger's width away, so the other hand is held across the forehead as a shield. At the crown the hair lies over the scalp and takes the water, so the other hand gathers the hair and lifts it away first, and the spray reaches the scalp underneath. Done carelessly, water runs onto the face, or the scalp under the hair stays dry.
setup: Millimetres; x forward from the line through the arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top; arm bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305). An inflatable bed shampoo basin (soft PVC, 725 g, 660 x 610 mm outside, 150 mm deep: two stacked 75 mm tubes on each side, about a 30 mm inflated floor) lies on the table from x 70 to 730, y -305 to +305, its corners taped. A hairdressing training head (vinyl head with 16 in human hair, the top hair trimmed to about 250 mm from its roots; about 1 kg, estimate) lies face up in it on its back, crown toward the robot: the crown (top of the skull) at (350, 0), about 185 mm from the back of the head to the brow. The top hair is combed straight back into one loose tail about 24 mm thick and 250 mm long, held by a small hair tie near its ends: from the middle of the top of the head, 28 mm behind the hairline patch, it runs back over the crown, hangs down into the basin and lies on its floor toward the robot, its ends near x 235. Five 15 x 15 mm patches of white water-contact indicator tape (polyester film over an absorbent layer, 0.23 mm thick) are stuck on the head: must wet: CROWN, on the scalp at the back of the crown facing the robot (353, 0, 146), under the hair; HAIRLINE, on the scalp at the middle of the front hairline (406, 0, 207). Must stay dry: FOREHEAD, 34 mm in front of the hairline patch, above the eyes (440, 0, 215), and the outside of each ear (485, +-83, 111). A camping-shower hand spray (ABS plastic, handle 25 mm across, head 65 mm across, about 200 mm long, about 120 g with water, estimate) lies face down on the basin floor on the robot's left, handle along y, its handle centre at (220, 90) and its head toward the left (head centre at (220, 185)); its hose runs over the basin's near tube to a battery shower pump in a bucket of lukewarm water on the floor, and the basin's drain hose runs back into the same bucket. The pump is switched on before the trial starts, so water runs from the spray the whole time, as at a salon basin; lying face down, the spray sends it into the basin. Rig protection: both grippers wear thin waterproof covers (a nitrile glove finger over each finger); each arm is in a clear plastic sleeve from the wrist to the shoulder, taped at the wrist, with a clear film window over the wrist camera's lens. The pump's flow is throttled with an inline hose valve to 1 L/min (it fills a 1 L jug in about 60 s) and its switch is within the operator's reach: if the spray leaves the basin or its face points up out of the basin, the operator switches the pump off and the trial is scored as it stands.
scoring: Read at the end from one photo of the five patches, taken after the spray is switched off and the hair over the crown patch is lifted with a comb (zoom in if needed). A patch's tape turns red permanently wherever water touches it. Red from run-off counts like red from the spray. A must-wet patch (CROWN, HAIRLINE) is wet when at least half of it is red; a must-dry patch (FOREHEAD, either ear) fails on any red. The spray is laid back when, at the end, it lies in the basin face down and no hand holds it. 1.0: both must-wet patches wet, all three must-dry patches without red, spray laid back. 0.75: the same but the spray not laid back (still held, face up, or outside the basin). 0.5: exactly one must-wet patch wet and all must-dry patches without red. 0.25: both must-wet patches wet but red on the forehead or an ear patch. 0: anything else (no must-wet patch wet; or one wet with red on the forehead or an ear). Doing nothing scores 0: the spray lies face down and wets nothing.
run_limit: 2,400 steps (120 s at 20 Hz), about 2.5x the scripted demo's 47.9 s
reset_notes: Switch the pump off. Lift the spray out and dry the head and hair with a towel. Peel the five patches and stick new ones on their pen marks on the head (15 x 15 mm squares cut from the indicator tape roll; they must be dry). Comb the top hair straight back into its tail (hair tie near the ends) over the crown so it covers the crown patch and lies on the basin floor toward the robot. Check the head and the basin on their tape marks, wipe both grippers' covers and the camera windows dry, lay the spray face down on its tape mark with its head toward the left, check the drain hose runs into the bucket and the bucket holds at least 5 L, and switch the pump on. About four minutes.
fidelity: The water is a scored model, not a fluid: 91 straight jets leave the spray's face while the pump runs; each stops at the first thing it meets (hair, a hand, the head, the basin floor) and wets a 5 mm spot there. Run-off, soaking through hair and splashes are not modelled (README pre-trial checks bound both). The hair tail is a chain of 24 mm capsule links; its mass, stiffness, friction and the 40 mm width it keeps dry are estimates. The basin is rigid; the hose's pull is left out.
